title: The sutras, closed
hookLine: a sick layman, a jeweled net, a pointing finger, a roadside Jizo

lines: A SICK MAN, A NET, A FINGER, A STONE.
cards: A sick man on a couch, in a room that keeps growing to fit his guests. A net of jewels, each one shining with all the others. A fingertip raised toward the moon.
A small stone figure by a road, wearing a red bib. Lay those four on a table and they don't look like they belong together. They came off one shelf.
When this stretch of the path began, the promise was modest: the Mahayana sutras are many, and i'd open a handful, in paraphrase. Today the handful goes back on the shelf.

teach.b: The sickroom. In the Vimalakirti Sutra, a layman is ill, and the Buddha's great disciples all find reasons not to visit. Manjushri goes, and the room makes space for everyone.
Vimalakirti says he is sick because the world is sick. Flowers fall and stick to those who think flowers improper. A goddess swaps bodies with Sariputra to show that male and female are not fixed.
And asked about non-duality, Vimalakirti answers with silence.
The net and the tower. In the Flower Garland, as the Huayan school explains it, each jewel in Indra's net reflects all the others.
Young Sudhana walks from teacher to teacher, a monk, a girl, a sailor, a king, and steps into Maitreya's tower, where every room holds every other. A world sits in a grain of dust.
The finger and the storehouse. The Lankavatara warns that words are a finger pointing at the moon, not the moon, and speaks of a storehouse where the seeds of habit are kept.
The ones who reach. The blue Medicine Buddha and his vows of healing. Ksitigarbha, who won't rest until the hells are empty, and who in Japan stands by the road as Jizo, guarding children.
Avalokiteshvara, turning his hearing around. A golden statue in rags.
A queen who teaches. Put together, the shelf has a shape. Again and again these books push against lines that seem fixed: lay and ordained, man and woman, sick and well, one thing and everything.
And again and again, someone reaches across.

how: Mahayana Buddhists in East Asia and Tibet keep, chant and study these sutras, and different communities give special place to different ones: the Vimalakirti among lay readers, the Flower Garland in Huayan and Kegon, the Medicine Buddha and Ksitigarbha sutras in temple devotion.

o: the rule books that monks and nuns must follow
short verses chanted only at memorial rites
discourses that set a teaching inside a scene

games.q: the sutras, closed: tap the pairs.
p: sick because the world is sick
each jewel reflects all the others
the finger is not the moon
stands by the road, guarding children

s: this stretch of the path read every Mahayana sutra
the promise was a handful, in paraphrase. the shelf is much longer.
in the Vimalakirti Sutra, a goddess swaps bodies with Sariputra
to show that male and female are not fixed.
Ksitigarbha and Jizo are two unrelated figures
in Japan, Ksitigarbha is known as Jizo.

games.q: you've heard a sick layman, a jeweled net, a pointing finger and a roadside stone. you can keep only one. how do you choose?
o: notice which one keeps coming back
games.why: today's practice: let the pictures pass and keep the one the mind returns to. and the finger and the moon say the image points past itself.

practice: Let the pictures from these weeks pass slowly, like books along a shelf: the falling flowers, the silent layman, the net of jewels, the tower, the finger and the moon, the red bib on a stone, the gold in rags.
Don't choose; notice which one the mind keeps coming back to. When one stays, let the others go, and rest with that one image.

wordCard.voice: The sutras. Discourses that open, thus have I heard, and set a teaching in a scene; in the Mahayana, a large library, of which this path has read a handful. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a discourse of the Buddha; in Pali, sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: the library, opened. Tomorrow the path turns from the shelf to the cushion. Shelf closed, for now.

sources.ref: Vimalakirti Nirdesa Sutra (the illness, the flowers, the goddess, the silence)

Lankavatara Sutra (the finger and the moon; the storehouse consciousness)
